I think this is exactly what he wanted, as these were the complaints levelled against the service when he was still in charge.

From 2018: https://drewdevault.com/blog/Signal/

> Moxie knows about everything I’ve said in this article. He’s a very smart guy and I am under no illusions that he doesn’t understand everything I’ve put forth. I don’t think that Moxie makes these choices because he thinks they’re the right thing to do. [...] Moxie can’t come out and say it openly, but he’s made the decisions he has made because they serve his own interests.

And it looks like it's working. The Signal social network is growing. Revenue is growing (revenue pays for ongoing maintenance). Alternative servers are not sapping user metrics. It's still easy to push both security fixes and eye-catching new features because one central server, and client upgrades are aggressively pushed. Spam is not a plague because registration remains expensive - you need a genuine phone number you control, or Google to vouch for you (who in turn have their own robust defences against account creation).

If it was a free sign up where you just need an IP address to play, spammers would have hundreds of millions of accounts and you'd get as much nuisance friend requests as you get email spam. Most people would leave. You've seen the scraperpocalypse, every sketchy person on the planet has money to fund a million sign ups each from a unique US residential IP (thanks to "smart" TV vendor neglect/corruption allowing residential proxies), IP reputation is worthless.

Personal instances of Signal would hide until spammers found them but you'd better have your own locked down registration because you can't hide forever. Not to mention that sending ongoing traffic to your own server tells everyone where and when you're posting, moreso than using Signal's centralised services.

Its tradeoffs all the way down.

>> I don't think this is what Moxie wanted.

You think, users should be required to carry a cell phone or make use of a debit card or credit card, in order to message another user, is exactly, what Matthew wanted?

That looks like crazy talk.

In that DEF CON 18 talk, Moxie talked about scope of choice and how the scope of choice changed to "do I want to carry a cell phone, or not?". A notion that Matthew's dream was to impose on the world a demand to carry a cell phone or a debit/credit card transaction on others, such a tax, to enjoy what he and his friends already had for free, is on its face absurd.

_

> Spam is not a plague because registration remains expensive

The issue of spam is fully mitigated with an invite token, a 16 byte string ; "is", not "can be", because other systems in production have already been doing this.

The way it works is simple. If Alice wants to receive a message from Bob, Alice can share a connection string username+token to Bob. Then Bob can message Alice and for that time not other users of the hosted centralized namespace.

Very simple concept.

Simple enough for a mediocre dev to implement without an LLM.

The spectre of spam does not justify the demand for a tracking device, nor the friction involved with an uninvolved and unwanted third party named Google (love Google overall but this is such a bastardly and disgusting concept), nor does it justify demanding a debit/credit card transaction become involved.

The spectre of spam does not justify any of this horse shit.

"Hey Bob, here is my username to message me, provided you subject yourself to this horse shit", where such horse shit antithetical in a fundamental way to the values espoused founder of Signal.

The new, grossly degenerated Scope of Choice.

Perhaps some who call themselves "hackers" or software developers may have been actually fooled by this false spectre of spam. I was never among them.

Even worse, the phone numbers, Google Play accounts, debit cards and credit cards, these are cheap. Among the scammer underworld these are a plenty and fungible.

An invite token personally sent by Alice or read aloud by Alice to Bob, is not.

But if somebody wants to harass a specific user on Signal, that's relatively cheap to do.

_

> Not to mention that sending ongoing traffic to your own server tells everyone where and when you're posting

Uncle Jeff, AWS, who doesn't tell exactly everyone but a lot of people, not excluding ICE at any given time, knows when you are posting, from where, and to what other users. The last of which is specifically obviated by a separate namespace hosted on a separate server.

On the occasions I have run Signal's server software, I and other users did mitigate these concerns. We do appreciate that others also have these means, or not.

Another messaging system, you may have already read its name actually, has already solved these problems in a way that they are successfully mitigated in a wholly transparent way for casual users.

_

> Its tradeoffs all the way down.

Right. In Matthew's view, the horse shit is a tradeoff.

I believe there are other tradeoffs available that are ethical, not more ethical, but ethical, and carry much less technical complexity.

nh2 · Oct 31, 2026

Or this case we encountered, where on iOS Signal apparently corrupts its sqlite DB, leading to loss of all messages.

https://github.com/signalapp/Signal-iOS/issues/5813

Interestingly here, the sqlite DB would be trivially fixable, and messages restorable, with the `sqlite3` CLI.

But there's no way to get at that sqlite DB file. Even if you change Signal's code to add a feature to export the DB, it apparently cannot see your DB, because iOS sandboxes that so that it is only visible to Signal builds signed with the Signal developers' keys.

So that means your messages are all there, on your device, running open-source software, and yet you cannot get them.

This cannot have been the intention of Signal being Free Software. Where is "change it to make it do what you wish (freedom 1)"?

(I do not use iOS myself but have friends suffering this issue. Everybody involved is programmers and yet we seem to be able to do nothing about it.)

So it seems that even though the messages are on the user's device, it really is the Signal developers who "own" that data, and have the exclusive and ultimate control over it.

Makes me wonder:

Does this mean users suffering this need to GDPR-request their data out from Signal?

palata · Oct 31, 2026

It explains perfectly why Signal does not want third-party clients.

To the haters: I am not saying that it is perfect, in an ideal world we could have secure third-party clients. I am just saying that it is pragmatic: in our world, we don't.

Signal has forever been a pragmatic approach to private messaging, and it succeeded at that: Signal literally put E2EE on the map!

Signal has a threat model, and they do the best app they can addressing that threat model. Which means that they cannot accept third-party clients or federation. They don't say "you cannot use XMPP or SimpleX or Matrix on the side", they just say "we provide this, if you benefit from it, use it for free".

Still, there is a very vocal minority that takes every opportunity they take to explain how "insane" that is, and how they "cannot imagine how anyone with some kind of intelligence wouldn't be revolted". I believe it is the same posture as those complaining about Android or GrapheneOS not giving root access ("even in the advanced settings"). The fact is that if you want root access on your phone, you should install a system that gives you root access, and not select a system that does not and then complain.

Signal is great at what it does. It's okay to also want something else while acknowledging that Signal is great at what it does.
